hashrate.title: From difficulty to hashrate
hashrate.p1: Each attempt succeeds with probability roughly target / 2²⁵⁶ ≈ 1 / difficulty. So on average the whole network needs about difficulty attempts per block, and if each block takes ~120 seconds:

intro: If twice as many GPUs suddenly joined the network, blocks would come twice as fast — unless the puzzle became twice as hard. Difficulty is the dial that keeps Ergo ticking at an average of one block every 2 minutes, no matter how many miners there are.

target.title: Target and difficulty
target.p1: In Autolykos, a solution is valid when the final hash — read as a 256-bit integer — is below a threshold called the target. The smaller the target, the harder it is. Ergo defines:
target.code:
target = q / difficulty
q = order of the secp256k1 group
  = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFEBAAEDCE6AF48A03BBFD25E8CD0364141
target.p2: Here q is just a fixed, enormous constant — about 1.16 × 1077, close to 2256. Dividing it by the difficulty gives the target: at today's difficulty of roughly 6 × 1013, only about one hash in 60 trillion falls below it.
target.p3: That makes difficulty the more intuitive number: doubling the difficulty means twice as many attempts are needed on average. And unlike Bitcoin (whose header stores the target), an Ergo header stores the difficulty itself, in compressed form.

nbits.title: nBits: squeezing a huge number into 4 bytes
nbits.p1: Difficulty can be a very large number, but the header only reserves 4 bytes for it. Ergo reuses Bitcoin's “compact” format: the first byte is the exponent (the length of the number in bytes), and the next 3 bytes are the mantissa (its first 3 significant bytes). To decode:
nbits.p2: Let's decode the nBits of the latest block and compare it with the difficulty reported by the explorer:
nbits.estimateText: Nobody can count the real hashrate. The explorer derives it from the difficulty alone (difficulty ÷ 120 s), so it only moves when the difficulty retargets and lags behind real changes in hashrate.

adjust.title: Difficulty adjustment
adjust.p1: Originally, Ergo recalculated the difficulty every 1024-block epoch using linear regression (linear least squares) over the last 8 epochs — predicting the hashrate trend rather than just looking at the previous epoch like Bitcoin does.
adjust.p2: Long epochs make the network slow to react when hashrate swings sharply (for example, when miners flock to another coin). So EIP-37 — activated in October 2022 at block 844,673 — changed the algorithm:
adjust.epoch: Epochs were shortened to 128 blocks (~4 hours 16 minutes), so difficulty is updated far more often.
adjust.average: The new difficulty is the average of the linear-regression prediction and a “Bitcoin-style” calculation based on the previous epoch.
adjust.cap: The change per adjustment is capped (roughly ±50%) to avoid overly large jumps.
adjust.p3: The exact details (coefficients, rounding) are in the EIP-37 specification and the reference node's source code. The key takeaway: the average block time is always pulled back to around 120 seconds.
